blood cardioplegic arrest and reperfusion with blood cardioplegia is more effective in salvaging myocardium after coronary artery occlusion than is reperfusion with unmodified blood alone.
cardioplegia is superior to cardiopulmonary by-pass for the preservation of myocardium at risk for infarction.
blood cardioplegic arrest and reperfusion of the ischemic zone results in better recovery of postischemic myocardial function than cardiopulmonary by pass with unmodified blood.

the role of cardioplegic arrest and reperfusion in the preservation of the heart during coronary artery surgery.
the development of a new technique to improve the quality of myocardial revascularization.
the development and application of a new technique to protect the human heart from the effects of ischemia.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
blood cardioplegic arrest during revascularization of the acutely evolving infarct provides better myocardial salvage than total vented cardiopulmonary support alone.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
blood cardioplegic arrest is the best method for arresting and protecting the heart during ischemic arrest, while total vented bypass is the best mode for reperfusion.
the cardioplegic arrest is a very important step in the process of revascularization, and it is not sufficient to simply open up the coronary artery.
cardioplegia is the preferred method of myocardial protection for patients with acute evolving myocardial ischemia.

blood cardioplegic reperfusion is more effective than total vented reperfusion in restoring postischemic myocardial function.
blood cardioplegic solution is a better way to preserve the heart during surgery.
